title: VanguardOps — On‑Prem Egress & RBAC Interop Review
summary: Deep dive on on‑prem network isolation, egress controls, RBAC/SSO integration, KMS handling for model keys, audit log capture and SOC2 evidence requirements. SE walked through proposed architecture and tradeoffs for an air‑gapped pilot vs VPC private control plane. Action: Redwood to share hardened runbook, SOC2 packet and sample diagram; customer to provide list of approved egress hosts and timeline for pilot (end of Q1).
topics: RBAC and SSO (SAML/OIDC) flow for private control plane
audit log collection and retention for SOC 2
KMS integration options (customer‑managed HSM vs Redwood KMS)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining — we're on for 52 minutes, appreciate you making time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Ethan Price: Ethan here, head of infra at VanguardOps. We run hybrid on‑prem clusters for regulated models.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Priya, security. Focused on SOC 2 controls and key provenance.
[00:16] Luis Gomez: Luis from Redwood SE, I'll walk through the on‑prem control plane options and egress patterns.
[00:22] Hannah Zhou: Hannah, solutions — I'll cover RBAC mapping and audit trails.
[00:26] Maya Patel: Great. Goal for the call: validate that our private deployment meets your SOC2 evidence needs and how RBAC/SSO will map to your IDP. Also discuss egress hardening.
[00:34] Samir Chaudhry: High level — our constraints: no outbound to internet except a small allowlist, we need KMS in our HSM, and we must retain all operator actions for seven years.
[00:43] Maya Patel: Understood. Luis, can you kick off the architecture?
[00:47] Luis Gomez: Sure. (screen) So two deployment patterns we see: 1) Private control plane with customer VPC peering — Redwood control plane in a private subnet ingesting telemetry over mTLS, or 2) fully air‑gapped on‑prem where the control plane is customer‑managed and we provide a packaged runtime. For egress we recommend a dedicated egress proxy that does TLS inspection and allowlists outbound endpoints: rectified endpoints include license check, metrics aggregator endpoint and optional model updates.
[01:10] Priya Nair: Wait — license check? We can't have anything like a phoning home that exposes request payloads.
[01:14] Luis Gomez: Right — the checks are metadata only, no payloads. We can design the agent to only send hashes and telemetry, and it can be configured to never send any PII or model input. We also have an option for handshake‑only egress where the agent performs a certificate handshake and then the rest of the control plane traffic goes over your private peering.
[01:30] Ethan Price: On the HSM side — we need to be able to rotate keys and show key provenance during audits. Can Redwood support wrapping model keys in our HSM (KMIP), or do you require Redwood KMS?
[01:38] Hannah Zhou: We support customer‑managed KMS. For on‑prem we have an integration layer that speaks KMIP and can store only the key encryption keys (KEKs) in your HSM. The runtime keeps ephemeral DEKs for inference in memory and never writes unencrypted model weights back to disk.
[01:51] Olivia Reed: Does that cover eDiscovery? If auditors ask for a trail, do you persist operator actions?
[01:56] Luis Gomez: Yes, we emit audit logs for all operator actions — rollouts, config changes, model pinning — and they can be forwarded to your SIEM (Splunk/ELK) over syslog or HTTPS with mutual TLS. Retention and export are configurable; we can also provide signed evidence bundles for SOC2 reviews.
[02:12] Samir Chaudhry: About RBAC — our IdP is Okta, we use SAML for SSO. We need role mappings to map Okta groups to Redwood roles and enforce least privilege.
[02:20] Hannah Zhou: We have a SAML/OIDC connector. Best practice is to provision SCIM groups for role sync and then apply RBAC in the control plane. We also support attribute based access so you can restrict by project tags. There's a caveat for on‑prem: if you run fully air‑gapped, you must host the auth connector on the customer side; Redwood provides a connector image you run behind your firewall.
[02:39] Priya Nair: How about service accounts? We need machine‑to‑machine tokens with fine grained scopes and automatic rotation.
[02:45] Luis Gomez: Service accounts support short‑lived tokens and can be minted via the control plane. For air‑gapped installs the token issuance flows are done by the local connector; tokens are signed by your KMS, so you retain control.
[02:56] Ethan Price: Regarding egress allowlist — what endpoints do we need to allow? Our security team will only approve a CIDR list.
[03:02] Maya Patel: We'll provide a hardened list. In general it's minimal: (1) attestation endpoint (metadata only), (2) metrics ingestion host, (3) optional model update mirror. We can also support a pull model where you mirror updates to your internal repo and block outbound entirely.
[03:18] Priya Nair: That pull model sounds better. Can you explain traffic flows for inference telemetry — does that include prompts or embeddings?
[03:25] Luis Gomez: No, telemetry is aggregate stats by default. We can configure redaction so no inputs or outputs are sent. For embeddings or trace payloads — those are never sent unless you opt in. The default is only token counts, latency histograms, error rates, and sampling of anonymized stack traces — no raw text.
[03:44] Samir Chaudhry: Firewall rules: do you require any inbound holes?
[03:47] Hannah Zhou: No inbound holes to worker nodes. If you use the private control plane, the control plane initiates connections outbound to the worker subnet over mutual TLS. For incoming API traffic from your apps, you'd route through an internal LB — Redwood runtime doesn't open public inbound ports by default.
[04:03] Priya Nair: How do we validate network segmentation? Auditors will want proof of egress filtering and host‑level hardening.
[04:09] Luis Gomez: We provide an attestation report and a runbook for deployment which includes iptables/ebpf baselines, kernel hardening checklists, and a network diagram with all flows. We can also run a joint validation where Redwood SE runs nmap/egress simulation from a bastion and provides results to your auditors.
[04:28] Olivia Reed: SOC2 evidence — what specifically will you hand us?
[04:32] Hannah Zhou: Typical packet: SOC2 Type II report, system architecture diagram, control mapping, encryption key lifecycle docs, sample audit logs trimmed for privacy, and KMS integration checklist. We also have a customer‑facing audit folder with signed manifests.
[04:46] Priya Nair: We need immutable logs. Can logs be routed to our WORM storage?
[04:50] Luis Gomez: Yes — logs can be forwarded to your append‑only store. We sign logs with a certificate chain so you can verify provenance. For long‑term retention we support exporting compressed, signed bundles monthly.
[04:59] Ethan Price: A practical question — latency. If we run models on local GPUs with a private control plane, what's typical token latency impact?
[05:05] Luis Gomez: For local GPUs and the runtime optimized kernels, the control plane adds negligible token latency — it's not in the token path. The only added hop is for cache prefetch/kv cache warmup when cold starts happen; warm requests are local. You should see no more than a few ms difference compared to direct local inference.
[05:20] Samir Chaudhry: Does your runtime use any third‑party modules that would break air‑gap policies?
[05:24] Hannah Zhou: The packaged runtime is self‑contained. Any optional telemetry or update agents are separate containers you can choose not to run. We ship a SBOM and a list of binary fingerprints for supply chain audit.
[05:35] Priya Nair: Can you show how RBAC works when an auditor requests access to specific logs? I'm worried about cross‑tenant visibility.
[05:42] Hannah Zhou: RBAC is tenant scoped. We support separation by namespace; auditors with read‑only roles can be granted limited scopes. We also generate auditor tokens that expire and are single use.
[05:51] Olivia Reed: What about data residency — we have EU users and the inference results must remain in EU. If we have a hybrid cluster, how do you enforce region pinning?
[05:59] Luis Gomez: We offer placement policies so workloads can be pinned to specific regions or subnets. For private deployments you control the compute location. If you use dedicated Redwood hosted model variants we can enforce region restrictions and provide contractual data residency guarantees.
[06:14] Ethan Price: For the pilot, we want to run a sample workload and measure telemetry while keeping all egress blocked except to our internal metrics endpoint. What's the minimal permissions you need?
[06:23] Maya Patel: Minimal: allow outbound to your internal metrics aggregator and KMS endpoints (if customer KMS). If you choose mirror updates, block outbound entirely and we won't send updates. We'll also need a service account in Okta or SCIM group for RBAC sync.
[06:36] Samir Chaudhry: Ok. Let's cover fallback policies — if local GPU pool is saturated, can requests failover to Redwood hosted variants?
[06:43] Luis Gomez: Yes, but that implies egress and data policies. We support tiered fallbacks with opt‑ins: (A) no fallback allowed, (B) fallback only to a private mirrored model in your cloud account, (C) fallback to Redwood hosted with strict data redaction. Any fallback to hosted must be explicitly enabled and approved by compliance.
[07:02] Priya Nair: For canaries and rollouts — we need auditability and quick rollback. How granular are rollouts?
[07:07] Hannah Zhou: Canary rollouts can be percent based, user based, or route based. Each rollout event is logged with actor, timestamp, and diff. Rollbacks are also atomic and recorded.
[07:16] Ethan Price: Will you share design diagrams and an example firewall rule set?
[07:19] Maya Patel: Absolutely. We'll attach a sample iptables/iptables‑nft/ebpf baseline and an egress proxy config.
[07:25] (crosstalk)
[07:27] Olivia Reed: Quick question about KV cache, we saw 'KV cash' in a previous doc — is the cache shared across tenants?
[07:31] Luis Gomez: No, KV cache is per tenant and per model instance. It's in memory on the worker, never persisted. We also have an option to disable KV cache for stricter compliance.
[07:40] Priya Nair: Can you produce a flow diagram that shows which data ever leaves our network? Auditors will want to see that explicitly.
[07:46] Luis Gomez: We'll produce a flow diagram and a CSV list of endpoints/ports for your firewall team.
[07:51] Maya Patel: Let's talk next steps and what we'll deliver by EOW.
[07:55] Hannah Zhou: Action items: share SOC2 packet, send SBOM and binary fingerprints, provide egress allowlist template, and an architecture diagram for pilot.
[08:05] Priya Nair: Also we need a proposed timeline — pilot start by March 15, full production by end of Q2 if tests pass.
[08:11] Maya Patel: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[08:14] (short pauses)
[08:17] Ethan Price: One last: what about encrypted swap? We need assurance the system never writes plaintext to disk even under memory pressure.
[08:23] Luis Gomez: Runtime uses mlock for sensitive buffers and will not swap secrets to disk. If node swap is enabled, the sensitive pages are encrypted; our deployment docs insist on swap disabled for worker nodes in high‑security configs.
[08:37] Olivia Reed: Great. Thanks everyone.
[08:40] Maya Patel: Thanks — we'll follow up with the packet.
[08:44] (meeting ends)
